divisions.question: That this bill be now read a second time. That this bill be now read a second time.

Bill—by leave—taken as a whole. Chris Ellison I table a supplementary explanatory memorandum relating to the government amendments to be moved to this bill. The memorandum was circulated in the chamber on 6 November 2006. Andrew Bartlett by leave—I move: (1) Schedule 1, item 3, page 3 (lines 25 and 26), omit “excusing, justifying, authorising, requiring or rendering less serious”, substitute “mitigating or enhancing the seriousness of”. (3) Schedule 1, item 5, page 4 (lines 22 and 23), omit “excusing, justifying, authorising, requiring or rendering less serious”, substitute “mitigating or enhancing the seriousness of”. These amendments go to roughly the same area and the same clauses as the government amendments. It would be fairly obvious to senators following the debate that they mirror recommendation 1 of the report of the Senate Standing Committee on Legal and Constitutional Affairs. I should say that, in moving these amendments, I do not resile from my previous comments that the legislation as a whole is unacceptable, but I think the least we can do is adopt the recommendations of the Senate committee report. I think the second recommendation is more important than the first, and I will speak to that one next. But these amendments go to and mirror recommendation 1. Joe Ludwig We divided on the second reading of the bill because Labor, as I said during the second reading debate, believes the [Crimes Amendment (Bail and Sentencing) Bill 2006](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/S529) is fundamentally flawed and should be rejected. Clearly, that is not going to be the case. We have now moved into the committee stage where the government is pressing ahead with a flawed bill. Senator Bartlett made the point that it is in his interests to try to improve the bill and it is in mine as well, given the circumstances which we now face. speeches.speaker: Sandy Macdonald
speeches.brief: Senator Coonan moved to introduce four bills: amending broadcasting law, the Broadcasting Services Act 1992, the Crimes Act 1914, and prudential regulation for trans-Tasman cooperation. The bills were agreed to and read a first time without formalities.

speeches.speaker: Sandy Macdonald
speeches.brief: The speaker introduced four bills: digital television reforms removing genre restrictions and phasing multichannelling for commercial broadcasters, with anti-siphoning protections maintained; media ownership reforms removing foreign ownership restrictions and relaxing cross-media rules while requiring minimum diversity of five media groups in capitals and four elsewhere, plus local content conditions; bail and sentencing amendments preventing customary law or cultural practice from mitigating criminal sentences or bail decisions; and trans-Tasman banking supervision amendments requiring APRA to support the Reserve Bank of New Zealand and consider financial system stability in New Zealand.

speeches.speaker: Kay Patterson
speeches.brief: The Legal and Constitutional Affairs Committee presented its report on the Crimes Amendment (Bail and Sentencing) Bill 2006, including the Hansard record and related documents, with an order for the report to be printed.

speeches.speaker: Joe Ludwig
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Crimes Amendment (Bail and Sentencing) Bill 2006 is fundamentally flawed, racially discriminatory in effect, and a distraction from ten years of failed Howard government Indigenous policy. The speaker stated the bill will have no impact on violence in Indigenous communities because federal law does not cover those offences, and criticised the government for removing cultural background from sentencing considerations without consultation or evidence.

speeches.speaker: Chris Ellison
speeches.brief: The speaker argued the Crimes Amendment (Bail and Sentencing) Bill 2006 is fundamentally flawed and rushed, and will not reduce Indigenous violence. They supported retaining 'cultural background' in sentencing factors, citing unanimous Senate committee recommendations and multiple Law Reform Commission reports, and criticised the government for hypocrisy and lack of consultation.

speeches.speaker: Chris Ellison
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the third reading of the Crimes Amendment (Bail and Sentencing) Bill 2006, arguing that passing it unamended repudiates the Senate Standing Committee on Legal and Constitutional Affairs' recommendation to retain cultural background as a sentencing factor, and criticised the government's record on Indigenous affairs.

The government moved amendments to remove "cultural background" as a factor in sentencing and forensic procedures, and to prohibit courts from using customary law or cultural practice to excuse, justify or lessen criminal behaviour.

speeches.speaker: Chris Ellison
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the removal of references to cultural background from bail, sentencing, and forensic procedures in the Crimes Amendment (Bail and Sentencing) Bill 2006, arguing the amendments were unrelated to the bill's stated purpose and the government had failed to consult. The government defended the changes as necessary for consistency and to prevent cultural background from being a factor in forensic procedures.
